headline: The official same-point comparison with 2022 slipped toward Republicans on Oct 22's files and now implies a national vote of about D-1.5 (±1.4) while the polls say D+8.7: by registration, Florida's early vote is D+1.7 against D+0.1 at 12 days out in 2022 after Republicans stretched their in-person lead to 50,000 ballots, Colorado is D+8.2 against D+3.2, Iowa's absentee pool D+21.2 against D+23.3, and Pennsylvania's mail ballots, matched to 2022 for the first time, are D+42.9 against D+53.4. Against 2024 the same files still read better for Democrats: Nevada D+4.1 against R+4.5 and Colorado D+8.2 against D+2.6 pool to about D+3.3 (±1.8), and Pennsylvania's mail is 12 points more Democratic than at this point in 2024. The news comparisons lean more Democratic: Jon Ralston's Nevada count has Democrats up 4.1 points with the mail D+9.4, North Carolina's early vote is 37% ahead of 2022 with registered Republicans barely above their 2022 count, Texas's first two days were 8-10 points more Democratic than 2024's by primary history (VoteHub), while Wisconsin's and Michigan's returns trail or barely match 2022.

measures.aff: Independent tracker of the official files; affiliation not stated. 33,418 ballots through Oct 15, mostly cast in person, vs. the same point in 2024 (D+10.4 at the same point in 2022)

measures.src: Call the Map (Maine Secretary of State absentee file), Oct 18
measures.aff: Independent tracker of the official file; affiliation not stated. 96,849 ballots through Oct 15 vs. the same point in 2024 (Oct 17, 2024); 2022 at the same working day was D+33.6

measures.src: Call the Map (Florida Division of Elections file), Oct 20
measures.aff: Independent tracker of the official file; affiliation not stated. 1,384,887 ballots through Oct 19 (mail 1,025,383, in person 359,504) vs. the same point in 2024, when in-person voting had also just begun; the count is 38% below 2024's. The app's own file reads D+4.3 on the same day

measures.aff: L2 is a nonpartisan commercial vendor; Virginia has no party registration, so party is modeled in both years

measures.src: News 5 Cleveland, Oct 13 (Ohio Secretary of State data)

compare_note: Registered-party margin among early ballots, 2026 vs. the same point in 2024, as read from the official files by Call the Map (an independent tracker; Iowa 33,418 ballots through Oct 15, Pennsylvania's 52 comparable counties through Oct 16, Maine 96,849 through Oct 15, Florida's 1,384,887 mail and in-person ballots through Oct 19 against R+4.9 at the same point in 2024). Virginia's early voters are 63% Democratic on L2's modeled two-party split, vs. 59% at the same point in 2024 (Morris, Oct 12); Ohio's early voters were 41% Democratic and 28% Republican by last primary ballot as of Oct 13, vs. 26% and 36% at this point in 2024 (News 5 Cleveland, from Secretary of State data). Florida's, Nevada's, Colorado's, Iowa's, Pennsylvania's and North Carolina's official comparisons with 2022 and 2024 are computed from the state files and run through Oct 22 (Nevada D+4.1 vs. R+4.5, Colorado D+8.2 vs. D+2.6, Iowa D+21.2 vs. D+4.2 and Pennsylvania D+42.9 vs. D+30.7 at this point in 2024). Every state with party registration is more Democratic than at this point in 2024, Florida included because 2024's Republicans had moved to the mail; against 2022 the picture is mixed and narrower, and Florida's in-person vote is now 50,000 ballots Republican.

bullets.title: The official comparison with 2022 now implies a national vote of about D-1.5; against 2024 it reads about D+3.3.
bullets.html: By registration, Florida's Oct 22 file counts 1,981,475 ballots at D+1.7 (mail 521,948 Democrats to 437,207 Republicans; in person 283,040 to 333,432), against D+0.1 at 12 days out in 2022, three days into in-person voting that year; Colorado's 726,213 returned ballots are D+8.2 against D+3.2 on the same day in 2022; Iowa's 51,288 mailed-back absentees are D+21.2 against D+23.3; and Pennsylvania's 723,055 returned mail ballots, matched to 2022 for the first time, are D+42.9 against D+53.4. The app's calibrated slopes turn those into +1.4, +4.2, -0.5 and -2.3 points of margin and a pooled implied national vote of about D-1.5 (±1.4), down from D-0.2 on Oct 21's files, against polls at D+8.7 and the app's forecast at D+6.8. Against 2024 the same files read better for Democrats: Nevada's Oct 22 file (284,851 ballots, 39.6% Democrats to 35.5% Republicans, D+4.1) against R+4.5, worth about +7.2, Colorado D+8.2 against D+2.6 (+4.7), pooling to about D+3.3 (±1.8); Pennsylvania's mail at D+42.9 against D+30.7 is worth about +2.7 (±3.4) and Iowa's D+21.2 against D+4.2 about +3.8 (±3.5). Arizona's county compilation reads D+0.5 on 743,697 ballots with no same-point baseline.
sources: Florida Division of Elections via the app's official comparison, Oct 22
UF Election Lab daily file (Nevada, Oct 22)
Pennsylvania Department of State daily mail-ballot report via the app's official comparison, Oct 22

bullets.title: Nevada: Democrats lead by 4.1 points after six days; mail D+9.4, in person R+4.7.
bullets.html: Jon Ralston's count on the evening of Oct 22 had 284,836 ballots cast, just under 14% of active voters, with Democrats ahead by 11,653, or 4.1 points: mail ballots D+16,675 (9.4 points) and in-person ballots R+5,022 (4.7 points), for an electorate of 40% Democrats, 35.5% Republicans and 24.5% others. He reprints his six-day post from 2022, when Republicans were winning Clark County's in-person vote by about 1.5 to 1, and writes that this year's pattern is 'not close' to that; after six days in 2024 Republicans led statewide by about 24,000 ballots. That morning the lead was about 11,300 (4.5%) of 244,767, with Clark 66% of ballots, Washoe 20% and the rurals 14%, Washoe and the rurals running 3-4 points above their share of active voters and Clark 7 below. Ralston: 'With any kind of party loyalty, an R would need significant indie advantages to win,' but he does not 'see all blue people, at least not yet.' The state's Oct 22 file reads D+4.1 against R+4.5 at this point in 2024.
sources: UF Election Lab daily file (Nevada, Oct 22)
bullets.aff: Nonpartisan outlet; county and Secretary of State data

bullets.title: North Carolina's early vote is 37% ahead of 2022; Democrats up 62%, Republicans 1.7%.
bullets.html: Michael Bitzer's Day 7 tally: 1,101,318 ballots, 302,540 (38%) more than the same day in 2022, with in-person voting up 325,800 (45%) and accepted mail down 23,260 (31%). By registration, Democrats have cast 452,221 ballots vs. 280,097 at this point in 2022 (up 62%), unaffiliated voters 356,594 vs. 207,710 (up 72%) and Republicans 239,079 vs. 235,174 (up 1.7%), so Republicans 'have finally broken even' with their 2022 count; Democrats and unaffiliated voters are 77% of in-person ballots, Republicans 23%. The Black share of the vote is 23% (24% in 2022), Boomers are 51%, Millennials 13% and Gen Z 6.4%, and the mail pool is older and whiter. His model projects 2.6-2.9 million in-person early votes and a combined 2.7-3.0 million, and he says the next ten days will show 'whether this opening surge ultimately translates into a significantly larger early-voting electorate or whether some of the increase reflects voters simply casting their ballots earlier.' The app's own file (1,269,919 accepted ballots through Oct 22, vs. 927,708 at this point in 2022) carries the official comparison.
sources: North Carolina State Board of Elections absentee file via the app's official comparison, Oct 22

bullets.title: Georgia passed 1.3 million ballots; in-person voting ran 12% ahead of 2022 at the state's last release.
bullets.html: The Secretary of State counted 1,007,015 in-person early ballots before noon on Oct 20, up 12% from 894,412 at the same point in 2022, plus 48,916 accepted absentee ballots. GeorgiaVotes.com's tally as of 7:15 a.m. Oct 22: 1,330,455 ballots, 1,267,737 in person and 62,718 by mail, which it puts 5% above 2022's same-point total of 1,268,916; Black voters 33.8%, white 53.0%; women 55.3%; voters 65 and over 46.5%; 214,717 (16.1%) did not vote in 2022. The AJC finds about 400,000 early voters from strongly Harris areas vs. 380,000 from strongly Trump ones (return rates 21% vs. 16%), rural South and Middle Georgia lagging and Republican Cherokee and Forsyth up on 2022; about 95% of early voters also voted in 2024. Georgia has no party registration.
bullets.aff: Official data; GeorgiaVotes is an independent tracker; AJC is nonpartisan

bullets.title: Texas: the first two days were 8-10 points more Democratic than 2024's by primary history.
bullets.html: Nearly 1.5 million Texans voted in the first two days of early voting. VoteHub's Zachary Donnini (CBS News Data Desk) says day one's electorate was 'about 10 points more Democratic than it was the first day of the 2024 in-person early voting' and day two eight or nine points more Democratic than the same day in 2024, with about 32% of Texans who have voted in Democratic primaries already voting against 21% of those with Republican primary history; VoteHub projects two-thirds of the vote will come early. The independent theoelections tracker counts 2,112,992 early voters through Oct 22 (1,954,543 in person, 158,449 by mail): 36.6% with only Democratic primary history, 34.2% only Republican, 25.7% neither, with the mail pool 39.0% to 25.9%. Republican consultant Derek Ryan's day-one report had Democratic-primary-only voters ahead by 69,046 where Republican-primary voters led by 81,429 on day one in 2022. Donnini: too early to draw conclusions, and a Republican-leaning state needs a strong Democratic electorate plus some Trump voters. Texas has no party registration.
bullets.aff: VoteHub works with the CBS News Data Desk; theoelections is an independent tracker whose affiliation is not stated; Derek Ryan is a Republican consultant

bullets.title: Florida: Republicans' in-person lead doubled to 50,000 as Democrats bank the mail.
bullets.html: The Division of Elections' Oct 22 file had 1,217,809 mail ballots returned, 521,948 from Democrats and 437,207 from Republicans (D+84,741), and 763,666 in-person ballots, 333,432 Republican to 283,040 Democratic (R+50,392, up from R+24,167 a day earlier); the combined gap narrowed from D+3.2 to D+1.7, against D+0.1 at this point in 2022, when in-person voting had been open three days. Every county must open sites by Oct 24. The News Service of Florida put turnout at about 11.7% of 13.7 million registered voters on Thursday morning's figures. Democratic consultant Steve Schale notes the state deleted its mail-request list, so every voter had to reapply; press comparisons are to 2022's final mail totals, not the same point.
sources: News Service of Florida via Central Florida Public Media, Oct 22
bullets.aff: Official data via a nonpartisan outlet; Schale is a Democratic consultant

bullets.title: Turnout without party: Wisconsin's returns trail 2022 by 15.6% despite a 65% first in-person day; Michigan's mail is 2% ahead.
bullets.html: Wisconsin: 257,777 absentee ballots returned including in-person absentee votes as of Oct 22, 15.6% fewer than the 305,453 at the same point in 2022 (WisPolitics, from Elections Commission data), after 55,659 voters cast in-person absentee ballots on Oct 20, the first day, vs. 33,644 in 2022; Dane and Milwaukee counties are 28.4% of the in-person vote (29.1% in 2022) and the Waukesha, Ozaukee and Washington suburbs 20.1% (23% in 2022). Michigan: 789,476 mail ballots returned as of Oct 20 vs. 771,967 at the same point in 2022 (up 2.3%), with 2,121,458 requests vs. 1,810,569 (up 17.2%), so 37.2% of requests are back against 42.6%; the Oct 21 dashboard showed 860,257 absentee ballots plus 804 early in-person votes, and statewide in-person voting opens Oct 24. Virginia had more than 568,000 early votes with 21 days to go vs. just over 307,000 in 2022 (VPAP), and Minnesota 202,252 accepted ballots through Oct 15 vs. 172,520.
sources: MITechNews (Michigan Secretary of State data), Oct 22

bullets.title: The Democratic edge is partly a change in how people vote, and Republicans say they vote later.
bullets.html: Mail is down and in-person voting up almost everywhere: North Carolina's mail ballots are 31% below 2022 while in-person is up 45%; Wisconsin's total returns are 15.6% below 2022 even though its first in-person day was 65% above; Pennsylvania's Democrats have requested 14% fewer mail ballots than in 2022 and returned 47% of them against 51% then, which Democratic strategist J.J. Abbott attributes to voters switching to in-person voting and Charles Stewart (MIT) says the data cannot explain; Michigan has 37% of requested ballots back against 43% in 2022. In Nevada, Ralston notes 2022's in-person voters switching to mail, and that Republicans won Election Day 2022 by 2-to-1; in Florida, Republicans lead the in-person vote by 50,000 while Democrats lead the mail by 85,000; in Texas, 63% of Democrats but 48% of Republicans plan to vote early (Texas Politics Project). UNC Charlotte's Eric Heberlig expects North Carolina Republicans to outvote Democrats on Election Day.
bullets.aff: Nonpartisan sources; Abbott is a Democratic strategist

calendar_note: Every Florida county must open in-person early voting by Oct 24 (counties could open Oct 19); Michigan's statewide sites, New York's and New Jersey's open Oct 24 and Kentucky's Oct 29. Texas, Alaska, Colorado's service centers and South Carolina opened Oct 19 and Wisconsin's in-person absentee voting Oct 20; Nevada's in-person early voting opened Oct 17, North Carolina's Oct 15 and Georgia's Oct 13. Georgia's and Texas's in-person periods end Oct 30, Maine's no-excuse absentee period Oct 29. Pennsylvania and New Hampshire have no early in-person voting.
cast_at_note: Ballots counted (UF Election Lab, 47 jurisdictions reporting, state data as of Oct 16-23) when these comparisons were compiled; sets the automatic early-vote weight.
signals_verdict: The official same-point comparison with 2022 (Florida, Colorado, Iowa and now Pennsylvania) implies a national vote of about D-1.5 (±1.4), down from D-0.2 a day earlier: Florida narrowed to D+1.7 by registration against D+0.1 at 12 days out in 2022 as Republicans won the in-person vote by 50,000 ballots, Colorado is D+8.2 against D+3.2, Iowa's absentee pool D+21.2 against D+23.3 and Pennsylvania's mail D+42.9 against D+53.4; against 2024, Nevada (D+4.1 vs. R+4.5) and Colorado pool to about D+3.3 (±1.8), so the early vote fits a Democratic year without confirming polls at D+8.7. Ralston's Nevada count is D+4.1 with mail at D+9.4 and in-person R+4.7, North Carolina runs 37% ahead of 2022 with Democrats up 62% and Republicans 1.7%, Texas's first two days were 8-10 points more Democratic than 2024's by primary history, and Wisconsin's returns trail 2022 by 15.6%. The next tests are Florida's first weekend with every county open from Oct 24, Michigan's in-person start the same day, whether Nevada's in-person Republican edge grows as the weekend crowd arrives, and Pennsylvania's mail gap against 2022 over the next week.

signals.title: Nevada Democrats lead by 4.1 points after six days: mail D+9.4, in person R+4.7
signals.value: Jon Ralston's count on the evening of Oct 22: 284,836 ballots cast (just under 14% of active voters), Democrats ahead by 11,653, or 4.1 points; mail ballots D+16,675 (9.4 points), in-person ballots R+5,022 (4.7 points); 40% Democrats, 35.5% Republicans, 24.5% others. He reprints his six-day post from 2022, when Republicans were winning Clark County's in-person vote by about 1.5 to 1, and calls this year's pattern 'not close' to that; after six days in 2024 Republicans led statewide by about 24,000 ballots. 'With any kind of party loyalty, an R would need significant indie advantages to win.'
signals.catch: Party is registration, not vote choice. Mail is about two-thirds of the vote and accounts for the whole Democratic edge; Republicans have won the in-person vote, and the weekend and Election Day crowds are theirs (2022's Election Day went Republican 2-to-1). Ralston does not 'see all blue people, at least not yet.' The state's own Oct 22 file reads D+4.1 against R+4.5 at this point in 2024 (the app's official panel); the 2022 baseline starts at 9 days out.
signals.aff: Nonpartisan outlet (Jon Ralston); county and Secretary of State data

signals.title: Georgia's early vote passed 1.3 million, 12% ahead of 2022 in person at the same point
signals.value: The Secretary of State counted 1,007,015 in-person early ballots before noon on Oct 20, up 12% from 894,412 at the same point in 2022, plus 48,916 accepted absentee ballots. GeorgiaVotes.com's file as of 7:15 a.m. Oct 22: 1,330,455 ballots (1,267,737 in person, 62,718 mail), 5% above its 2022 same-point figure of 1,268,916; Black voters 450,090 (33.8%), white 704,902 (53.0%); women 55.3%; voters 65 and over 46.5%, 18-29 7.0%; 214,717 (16.1%) did not vote in 2022.
signals.catch: Georgia has no party registration, so this is turnout, not direction. Mail is a far smaller share than in 2022, which flatters the in-person comparison; the tracker's all-ballot comparison (+5%) is much smaller than the state's in-person one (+12%) and its 2022 basis is not stated. The AJC reports turnout lagging in rural South and Middle Georgia and up in Republican Cherokee and Forsyth; about 95% of early voters also voted in 2024.
signals.src: Georgia Secretary of State, Oct 20; GeorgiaVotes.com, Oct 22; AJC, Oct 20
signals.aff: Official data; GeorgiaVotes is an independent tracker of the state file; AJC is a nonpartisan outlet

signals.title: Ohio's early electorate has flipped from Republican to Democratic
signals.value: Democrats have returned about 94,000 ballots, unaffiliated voters a little more than 67,000 and Republicans nearly 64,000 (by last primary ballot), per the Ohio Capital Journal from Secretary of State data through Oct 12-13; News 5 Cleveland put Democrats at 41% and Republicans at 28% of nearly 230,000 early votes as of Oct 13, vs. 26% and 36% at this point in 2024. In-person votes after one week: 194,841 vs. 50,368 in 2022. On Point Politics counts 764,330 ballots cast through Oct 21 (319,992 mail, 444,338 in person), without party.
signals.catch: 2024 was a presidential year, and Ohio Republicans are shifting from mail to later voting: mail requests are 631,079 vs. 871,041 at this point in 2022. 'Party' is the last primary ballot pulled; seniors are more than half of ballots so far. No newer party breakdown has been published since Oct 15.
signals.src: Ohio Capital Journal (Ohio Secretary of State data), Oct 15; News 5 Cleveland, Oct 13

signals.title: Virginia's early vote is nearly 300,000 ballots ahead of 2022
signals.value: More than 678,000 Virginians had voted by Oct 18, nearly 300,000 more than at the same point in the 2022 midterm (VPAP data via WTVR). Danville has 2,800 vs. a little over 1,000 in 2022.
signals.catch: Virginia has no party registration, so this is turnout, not direction. The count's exact as-of day is not stated. The modeled party lean is in the separate L2 signal.
signals.src: WTVR CBS 6 (Virginia Public Access Project data), Oct 18
signals.aff: Nonpartisan outlet; VPAP is a nonpartisan tracker of state data

signals.title: Maine's absentee vote is 37% ahead of 2022 and slightly more Democratic
signals.value: 126,998 ballots through Oct 19 (67,843 by mail, 68,223 in person): 66,690 Democrats (up 34% on 2022), 25,106 Republicans (up 24%), 35,202 unaffiliated (up 57%). That is a D+32.7 gap vs. D+32.0 at the same working day in 2022; the count is up 37%. Through Oct 15 the gap was D+34.2 vs. D+21.7 at the same point in 2024.
signals.catch: Registration is not vote choice. The edge over 2022 is less than a point and has narrowed as in-person absentee voting (half the ballots) grows. The 2022 match is by working day.
signals.src: Call the Map (Maine Secretary of State absentee file), Oct 20
signals.aff: Independent tracker of the official file; affiliation not stated

signals.title: Minnesota's accepted ballots are running 17% ahead of 2022
signals.value: 202,252 absentee and mail ballots accepted through Oct 15 (80,870 in person, 121,382 by mail), vs. 172,520 at the same point in 2022. 519,813 ballots distributed vs. 474,935.
signals.catch: Minnesota has no party registration, so this is turnout, not direction. The lead over 2022 has narrowed from 29% (Oct 8). The source is a local news aggregator citing the Secretary of State's Oct 16 report; the report itself was not opened.
signals.src: Minneapolimedia News (Minnesota Secretary of State Oct 16 report), Oct 18
signals.aff: Official data via a local aggregator

signals.title: Pennsylvania Democrats' mail requests are down 14% on 2022 and fewer of them are back
signals.value: Votebeat/Spotlight PA: about 1.2 million approved mail ballots as of Oct 19, fewer than at the same point in 2022 or 2024; requests from Democrats are down 14% on 2022 and Republicans' up 11%; Democrats have returned 47% of theirs (51% in 2022, 55% in 2024), Republicans 43%, independents 36%. The state's Oct 22 file has 723,055 ballots returned of 1,223,893 approved (792,966 Democratic requests, 296,904 Republican); the app's official panel reads D+42.9 against D+53.4 at this point in 2022 and D+30.7 in 2024.
signals.catch: Pennsylvania's mail vote is lopsidedly Democratic every year (D+53 at this point in 2022, when Republicans won the national vote), and Democrats are shifting to Election Day voting after the party's own warnings about the mail (Charles Stewart: the data cannot show the cause). Older voters dominate the returns so far; the official comparison is on the app's panel, so this signal is the request and return-rate picture only.
signals.src: Votebeat/Spotlight PA, Oct 20; Pennsylvania Department of State daily report, Oct 22
signals.aff: Independent tracker of the official file; Votebeat and Spotlight PA are nonpartisan newsrooms

signals.title: Wisconsin's absentee returns trail 2022 by 15.6% even after a 65% first in-person day
signals.value: 257,777 absentee ballots returned, including in-person absentee votes, as of Oct 22, 15.6% fewer than the 305,453 at the same point in 2022 (WisPolitics, from Elections Commission and MyVote data); 55,659 voters cast in-person absentee ballots on Oct 20, the first day, vs. 33,644 in 2022, a 65% jump. Dane and Milwaukee counties are 28.4% of the in-person vote (29.1% in 2022); Waukesha, Ozaukee and Washington are 20.1% (23% in 2022). Mail ballots received as of Oct 20 were down nearly 26% from 2022 (WPR).
signals.catch: No party registration. Reporting lags (Elm Grove showed zero in the state data against 215 per its clerk), and Mordecai Lee (UW-Milwaukee) attributes the mail decline to worries about the Postal Service and Trump's executive order, so much of it is a mode shift; both parties have pushed voters away from mail. The gap may close in person over the next ten days.
signals.src: WisPolitics (Wisconsin Elections Commission data), Oct 22; WPR, Oct 21

signals.title: Michigan's mail returns are 2% ahead of 2022, requests 17% ahead, so a smaller share is back
signals.value: 789,476 ballots returned as of 7 a.m. Oct 20 vs. 771,967 at the same point in 2022 (up 2.3%), on 2,121,458 requests vs. 1,810,569 (up 17.2%), so 37.2% of requested ballots are back against 42.6% in 2022 (Secretary of State data via MITechNews); the Oct 21 dashboard showed 860,257 absentee ballots returned plus 804 early in-person votes, without a 2022 comparison.
signals.catch: Michigan has no party registration, so this measures turnout, not direction. About 94% of requests come from the permanent mail list, which inflates the request count; returns had been 30% ahead of 2022 on Oct 6 and have since converged. Statewide in-person early voting opens Oct 24.
signals.src: MITechNews (Michigan Secretary of State data), Oct 22
signals.aff: Official data via a nonpartisan outlet

signals.title: Texas: the first two days were 8-10 points more Democratic than 2024's by primary history (VoteHub)
signals.value: Nearly 1.5 million Texans voted in the first two days. VoteHub's Zachary Donnini: day one's electorate was 'about 10 points more Democratic than it was the first day of the 2024 in-person early voting,' and day two eight or nine points more Democratic than the same day in 2024; about 32% of Texans with Democratic primary history have voted against 21% of those with Republican primary history. theoelections' count through Oct 22: 2,112,992 early voters, 36.6% with only Democratic primary history and 34.2% only Republican (in person 36.4% to 34.9%; mail 39.0% to 25.9%). Derek Ryan's day-one report had Democratic-primary-only voters ahead by 69,046 where Republican-primary voters led by 81,429 on day one in 2022.
signals.catch: No party registration: 'party' is primary history, which covers about three-quarters of early voters, and the baseline is a presidential year. Donnini says it is too early to draw conclusions and that a Republican-leaning state needs a strong Democratic electorate plus some Trump voters. The Texas Politics Project finds 63% of Democrats but 48% of Republicans planning to vote early, so early surges may fade; Ryan is a Republican consultant, theoelections' affiliation is not stated.
signals.aff: VoteHub works with the CBS News Data Desk; theoelections is an independent tracker; Derek Ryan is a Republican consultant

signals.title: Florida Republicans' in-person lead doubled to 50,000 after four days while Democrats lead the mail by 85,000
signals.value: Division of Elections file for Oct 22: 763,666 in-person ballots, 333,432 Republican, 283,040 Democratic, 147,194 other or no party (R+50,392, up from R+24,167 the day before); 1,217,809 mail ballots returned, 521,948 Democratic, 437,207 Republican (D+84,741). The combined gap narrowed from D+3.2 on Oct 21 to D+1.7, against D+0.1 at this point in 2022.
signals.catch: Only counties that chose to open early are voting; all must by Oct 24. Republicans won Florida's in-person vote by far more in 2022 and 2024, and 2022's in-person voting had been open three days at this point, so the same-point comparison already includes some of that; no same-point in-person figure for 2022 was published. Registration is not vote choice. The overall same-point comparison is the app's official panel.
signals.src: Florida Division of Elections daily file via the app's official comparison, Oct 22

signals.title: Clark County's mail vote is less Democratic than at this point in 2022
signals.value: Clark County mail ballots through Oct 18: 46,590, Democrats 19,681 (up 3% on 2022), Republicans 13,459 (up 34%), others 13,450 (up 34%), a D+13.4 gap vs. D+23.2 at the same number of days before Election Day in 2022; the count is up 19%. Of 97,990 Clark ballots in the file, 62% were mail and 38% in person (Call the Map). Ralston has Clark's mail at 43-29.
signals.catch: Democrats are shifting from mail to in person, which Ralston's county-wide figures (Clark D by nearly 12 overall) absorb; this compares only the mail mode. Registration is not vote choice. Small numbers for a county of 1.4 million voters.
signals.src: Call the Map (Clark County mail file), Oct 20
signals.aff: Independent tracker of the official file; affiliation not stated
